live.spec_caveat: Quick look: a 3 × 3-pixel sum minus the local background, multiplied by a per-detector aperture correction measured on isolated stars. It is accurate to about 4% for a star at the centre of the view; elsewhere a star that falls between pixels can read up to 10% low. Flagged pixels are not masked, and crowded sources are not separated. For measurements, use IRSA's SPHEREx Spectrophotometry Tool.

cand.about_nn: Marked by a small neural network, and only where both of SPHEREx's simultaneous pictures (one short-wave, one long-wave detector) show something at the same spot, so cosmic rays and bad pixels, which hit one picture only, are left out. Marks found: {n}, strongest first. On real asteroids in 16 new fields it marked 71 of 147 sightings brighter than magnitude 17.5 (three in four of those brighter than 16), more than any other method we tested, at about 3 false marks per 100 pictures. It misses many fainter ones.
cand.about_z: Ranked by how strongly each spot differs from the median of the other pictures from the same detector, at a setting where about 3 false marks are expected per 100 pictures. Marks found: {n}, strongest first.
cand.about_uncal: The {n} spots that differ most from the median of the other pictures from the same detector, in rank order. Unfiltered ranking: the top of the list is often cosmic-ray hits and hot pixels, which single pictures contain.
cand.none: Nothing passed the threshold in these pictures.
cand.none_uncal: No spot differs from the other pictures by 3σ or more.

tm.lede: Epoch plays every picture NASA's SPHEREx telescope has taken of any spot in the sky, in time order, and flags what changed. It is built for volunteers who search survey images, for students and teachers, and for astronomers who want to check a position before downloading the data.
intro.open: Open it in the time machine
tour.btn: New here? Take the tour (1 minute)
tour.s_idea: NASA's SPHEREx telescope photographs the same spots in the sky again and again. Epoch lines those pictures up in time order, so you can see what moved or changed. These two pictures of Barnard's Star, taken 15 years apart, show the idea: the star has moved.
tour.s_picture: This is a small patch of sky. Each square is one pixel, and the bright blobs are stars. The picture changes as you move through time.
tour.s_play: Press Play to flip through every picture of this patch, or use the arrows (or the ← and → keys) to go one picture at a time.
tour.s_timeline: Each stripe is one picture, from the first date on the left to the last on the right. Its colour shows which infrared colour the picture was taken in: SPHEREx sees a slightly different colour each time.
tour.s_views: A star looks brighter in some infrared colours than in others, so flipping through every picture makes ordinary stars flicker. “One detector at a time” shows only pictures taken in similar colours, so most of that false flicker disappears and real changes stand out.
tour.s_counts: This counts the spots that changed more than expected. Compare the two views: flipping through every picture flags far more, and almost all of those are false.
tour.s_candidates: A small neural network marks the spots most likely to be real changes, strongest first, and only where both of SPHEREx's simultaneous pictures show something. It finds many real changes but misses some, and a few marks are false. Click a date to see that picture, then Keep or Dismiss it. You can download the ones you keep as a table.
tour.s_markers: Marks on the picture show known stars, known asteroids, variable stars, flaws in the picture, and changes nobody has explained yet.
tour.s_any: Type any position on the sky, or pick one of the targets, to load every SPHEREx picture of it straight from NASA's public archive. After loading, Epoch lists possible real changes for you to check.
tour.s_more: Results describes what we found with these pictures, and Methods explains how, in detail.
intro.caption: Barnard's Star, the fastest-moving star in the sky, moved 2.7 arcminutes between these two pictures, almost a tenth of the width of the full Moon. The circle marks the star; the cross marks where it is in 2025.
intro.alt: Barnard's Star in a NASA WISE picture from 2010 and a NASA SPHEREx picture from 2025
live.more_h: More tools: add, subtract, compare with WISE, follow a moving object, Gaia stars
live.changes_differ: These counts are measured live in your browser, on the field of view you chose, without the archive's quality flags. They are a different measurement from the prepared fields, and they can change slightly between loads if some pictures fail to download. Pipeline pixel flags for each picture are shown on the prepared fields.
